text: Implement a first-in, first-out queue using only stack operations. Support push to the back, pop and peek from the front, and empty. Follow-up: make every operation amortized constant time.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. I may only use stack operations, so I'll use two stacks: in takes pushes, out serves pops. Push goes to in, in constant time. For pop or peek, if out is empty, I pour in into out. That reverses the order once, so out's top is the oldest element, the queue front. I only transfer when out is empty, so each element moves once, which gives amortized constant time. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Why is out's top the front?

The newest element sits on top of in. Popping in's top over and over into out reverses them, so the oldest ends up on top of out. That's exactly the queue front. One reversal turns last-in, first-out into first-in, first-out.

This problem reminds me of lazy evaluation with amortized analysis: put off the expensive work until it's actually needed, and make sure each element pays for it only once. The lazy part is essential. I transfer only when out is empty. If I moved elements back and forth on every operation, each one would be linear. Instead, each element is poured once and consumed from out, never returning to in.

Here's the plan. One: push goes onto in. Two: peek drains in into out if out is empty, then returns out's top. Three: empty means both stacks are empty. One thing worth flagging — pop just calls peek, then pops out. Reusing peek keeps the when-to-transfer logic in one place.

Alright, let me code this up. Stack one is in and stack two is out. Push only touches in. Peek holds the transfer: if out is empty, it moves everything from in to out, which reverses the order, then returns out's top. Pop calls peek first, so out is guaranteed to have the front, then pops it. The line to get right is the guard on the transfer: pour only when out is empty. Pouring while out still holds elements would bury the older ones under newer ones and break the order. And empty must check both stacks, since elements can sit in either one.

Let's dry-run the code. Push one, two, three, then pop, push four, pop, pop — expected one, two, three. The row that matters is the first pop: out is empty, so I drain in, and out becomes three, two, one with one on top. It returns one. After push four, out still has items, so the next two pops don't transfer. They return two and three, while four waits in in until out empties. Each element is poured at most once. That matches.
A single pop can be linear. Justify amortized constant time.

Each element takes a fixed tour: a push onto in, one transfer to out, and one pop from out. That's a constant number of stack operations, done once. Over n operations, that's linear total work, so constant time amortized. The occasional expensive pop just settles up for the cheap pushes that came before it.

Let me think about complexity here. Push is constant. Pop and peek are amortized constant, with a worst case of linear for a single call. Space is linear for the two stacks. The mirror problem, a stack built from queues, doesn't get this with the rotate approach: rotating the queue redoes work on every push, because the old elements keep cycling around. Here the reversal happens once and flows one way, which is what makes lazy transfer amortize cleanly.
Excellent. The reversal insight, the lazy transfer, pop reusing peek, and a crisp amortized argument. Done.
